title: Terrine de Campagne
subtitle: French country pork and liver terrine
excerpt: Terrine de campagne is a French country-style pork terrine made with pork mince, chicken livers, lardons, herbs, and brandy, baked in a loaf tin set in a water bath. It is sliced cold, served with cornichons, Dijon mustard, and bread. Making it a day ahead is not optional: the terrine needs time to set and for the flavour to develop.
sourceNotes: Terrine de campagne (country terrine) is a fundamental preparation of French charcuterie. The combination of pork, liver, and aromatics cooked in a terrine mould is documented in the French culinary tradition from the 18th century, though home versions became common in the 20th century.

recipe.freezeNotes: Slice and freeze between baking parchment. Defrost overnight in the fridge.
recipe.batchNotes: Scales easily. Make two terrines at the same time.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Must be made at least 8 hours ahead (overnight is better). Keeps in the fridge for up to 5 days.

content.text: A terrine de campagne has three components: coarsely textured pork mince that provides the bulk, chicken livers that add richness and depth of flavour, and lardons that provide fat and salinity. The whole thing is seasoned aggressively: terrines cool to eating temperature in the fridge, and cold food needs more seasoning than hot. Use the back of a spoon to taste the raw mixture and adjust.

items.prepNote: not too lean, at least 20% fat

content.text: Roughly chop the chicken livers and mix with the pork mince, lardons, onion, garlic, brandy, thyme leaves, and eggs. Season very generously with salt and pepper: a terrine needs noticeably more seasoning than a hot dish because it is eaten cold. Fry a small amount of the mixture in a pan to taste and adjust. The mixture should taste properly savoury.

Heat the oven to 160°C fan. Line a 1-litre loaf tin with the streaky bacon slices, overlapping and draping them over the sides. Fill with the terrine mixture, pressing it down firmly to eliminate air pockets. Fold the bacon over the top. Place the bay leaves on top.

Place the loaf tin in a deep roasting tin. Pour boiling water into the roasting tin to come halfway up the sides of the loaf tin (a bain-marie). Cover the top of the loaf tin with foil. Bake for 1 hour 15 minutes to 1 hour 30 minutes until a skewer inserted into the centre comes out hot and the juices run clear.

Remove from the water bath and cool to room temperature. Place a weight on top of the foil (a second loaf tin filled with tins is ideal) and refrigerate overnight. This pressing firms the texture and helps it slice cleanly.

items.cause: Not enough fat in the mixture, or it was not pressed and chilled for long enough
items.fix: Use pork mince with at least 20% fat. Press with a weight overnight rather than just a few hours.

items.symptom: Terrine tastes bland when eaten cold
items.cause: The mixture was seasoned as if it were a hot dish, not accounting for flavour muting at cold temperatures
items.fix: Season the raw mixture heavily and fry off a small piece to taste before filling the tin.

content.text: Turn out onto a board, slice thickly, and serve with crusty bread, cornichons, and Dijon mustard. A terrine de campagne is the centrepiece of a French charcuterie board. It keeps well for 5 days in the fridge, making it very practical for entertaining.
